extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent attorneys, and law students working on patent litigation and evidence
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria for proving title, novelty, utility, sufficiency of specification, infringement, and damages in patent litigation; addresses who may be witnesses, burdens of proof, and what kinds of proof are competent. Geared to presentation and assessment of evidence at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who decides novelty and patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty of the invention is a prerequisite to validity and is a question of fact; upon all the facts attending the alleged invention, it is for the court to settle whether it is a patentable subject, but novelty itself is a question of fact to be determined (often by the jury) under judicial guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court settles whether the subject is of a sort which law will protect; novelty is a fact question to be tried under proper instructions. (Text: 'the novelty of the invention is a prerequisite ... and this is a question of fact ... it is still to be determined whether it is that species of invention to which the law gives the protection of a patent.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue of infringement = substantial identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of infringement is whether the defendant's invention is substantially the same thing as that of the plaintiff; identity/diversity is a matter of fact depending on evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of identity is for the jury under proper instructions; the court cannot itself simply declare the two identical by comparing devices without juror fact finding. (Text: 'whether the invention of the defendant is substantially the same thing as that of the plaintiff...it is for the jury to determine, as matter of fact...whether the two things are the same or different.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's license under another patent is not a complete defense
rubrics_metrics.description: On infringement the issue is between the plaintiff's machine as described in his patent and the machine made/used/sold by defendant; it is no answer for defendant to show he is a licensee under another patent and his machine is made in accordance with that patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being a licensee under a different patent does not absolve infringement of plaintiff's patent. (Text: 'it is no answer for the defendant to show that he is a licensee under another patent...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Two primary categories of evidence in patent causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence in patent litigation divides into (1) evidence of title and (2) evidence of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of title relates to letters-patent, plaintiff's interest, novelty, utility, and specification sufficiency; evidence of infringement relates to identity of defendant's thing with the patentee's invention. (Text: 'The evidence appropriate ... may be divided into (1) the evidence of title, and (2) the evidence upon the point of infringement.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Certified letters-patent as competent evidence of grant
rubrics_metrics.description: A copy of the letters-patent under the Patent Office seal and commissioner signature is competent evidence that a patent has been granted for the invention described in the annexed specification (per statute of 1836 §§4,5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent refers to a description in a former patent, that former patent must be produced and read to show what the invention is if the present patent does not make it clear. (Text: 'makes a copy under the seal of the Patent Office and the signature of the commissioner competent evidence...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue and extension actions of the commissioner are conclusive (except fraud/jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where patentee surrendered original patent and took a reissue with amended specification, the commissioner's action in granting the reissue is conclusive evidence on inadvertence/accident/mistake and not re-examinable except for fraud or evident want of jurisdiction; same for extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissioner's determinations are conclusive in courts except for fraud or jurisdictional defects. (Text: 'the action of the commissioner ... is conclusive evidence ... not re-examinable elsewhere, except upon the ground of fraud or evident want of jurisdiction.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent is prima facie evidence of first inventor; burden on challenger
rubrics_metrics.description: Once letters-patent are proved to have issued, they are prima facie evidence that the patentee was the first inventor; the burden of proof rests on any party who objects to show the grant was improperly obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the patentee swore to being first inventor before issuance, law presumes regularity and satisfactory proofs to the officers. (Text: 'they are prima facie evidence that the patentee was the first inventor...the burden of proofs is cast upon the party who would object.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant asserting equitable title must plead and prove it distinctly
rubrics_metrics.description: If defendant wishes to set up a merely equitable title against one with full legal title, he must distinctly allege such a defense in his answer and establish it on the title; the burden of proof is against him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable-title defenses require explicit pleading and proof. (Text: 'he must distinctly allege such defence in his answer, and establish it on the title. The burden of proof is against him.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible negative evidence of prior knowledge (testimony of those 'in the way of hearing')
rubrics_metrics.description: To rebut charges that patentee was not first inventor, plaintiff may call persons who would likely have heard of the invention if it had existed before, to testify they had not heard of it; this negative evidence helps prove novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plaintiff's task is to prove a negative (invention did not exist before) by exhausting affirmative instances; the more such witnesses were in the way of hearing of the invention, the stronger the evidence. (Text: 'he can only call persons who were in the way of hearing of the invention...to testify that they have not heard of it.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of absence-of-knowledge testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony that knowledgeable persons had not heard of the invention is general and negative but carries weight—especially where prior efforts of others suggest near-completion but not actual completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior efforts rested in experiment only, those experiments do not prevent later valid patents; jury must decide whether prior efforts reached completion. Evidence that invention was never heard of until patentee's disclosure is of great weight. (Text: 'Although this evidence is only general and negative, it is not, on that account, without weight.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior experiments vs completed invention (experiments alone insufficient to defeat later patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: If prior inventor's efforts were only experiments (even if near the result), those experiments will not prevent a subsequent inventor who produced the complete result from obtaining a valid patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must decide whether prior efforts 'rested in experiment alone' without completion, considering whether invention had been heard of in the trade. (Text: 'if the prior efforts ... rested in experiment alone, his experiments ... will not prevent a subsequent, more successful inventor...from obtaining a valid patent.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations by the patentee (res gestae) as evidence of completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee may give in evidence his own declarations describing nature and object of invention (as part of the res gestae) to fix the time when the invention was completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conversations and declarations, coupled with description of details, are legitimate to fix origin at least as of that period. However, if the inventor has assigned away his interest, subsequent declarations are inadmissible to affect assignee's rights. (Text: 'the patentee may give in evidence his own declarations, as part of the res gestae... but where the inventor has parted with his interest ... any subsequent declarations ... are wholly inadmissible.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Same evidentiary principles apply when novelty question involves identity/diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: When novelty involves comparing the patented thing with something previously known, the nature and sources of evidence are the same as when identity/diversity arises on infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles of evidence for identity/diversity under infringement apply to novelty disputes about identity. (Text: 'The nature of the evidence, and the sources from which it is to be drawn, are the same ... as when the question of identity or diversity arises under the issue respecting an infringement.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee cannot abandon or prove a part of a combination useless at trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patent is for a combination, the patentee is not permitted, on the trial, to abandon part of the combination as useless, nor to prove it useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combination patent must stand or fall as claimed; patentee cannot drop elements opportunistically at trial. (Text: 'Where the patent is for a combination, the patentee is not permitted, on the trial, to abandon a part of the combination as useless, still less can he be suffered to prove it useless.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of damages must be direct and specific
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of a license fee, actual damages must be proved by evidence bearing directly on the point, so that the jury are furnished with sufficient data and not left to guess probable damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages proof should provide concrete data; do not leave jury to exercise their ingenuity in guessing. (Text: 'actual damages must be proved by evidence bearing directly on the point... not left to the exercise of their ingenuity in guessing probable damages.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff must offer some evidence of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must offer some evidence that the invention is capable of some use beneficial to society; degree of utility is immaterial but some useful purpose must be shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility may be shown by testimony of persons conversant with the subject, by large public orders, or licenses taken; witnesses may attest whether article is capable of the designed use or is an improvement. (Text: 'The plaintiff must also offer some evidence of the utility of his invention...ordinarily proved by the evidence of persons conversant with the subject...or by other testimony ... that large orders have been given ... or that licenses have been taken.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff must offer evidence of sufficiency of specification (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must show the specification is 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, as to enable any person, skilled in the art or science to which it appertains, to make, construct, compound, or use' the thing patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where invention is complicated or uses terms of art, plaintiff should give evidence that the specification can be applied by those addressed; if sufficiency is disputed, plaintiff must go into evidence to sustain it. Slight evidence at first is generally sufficient to shift burden to defendant to falsify. (Text: 'he must show... that his specification is "in such full, clear, and exact terms..."')

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper witnesses to determine specification sufficiency: practical workmen of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general standard, the ability of skilful practical workmen in the particular branch of industry to practise the invention from the directions in the specification is the test of sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard varies by subject-matter: e.g., pump—an ordinary pump-maker; composition—practical chemist of ordinary skill; process applying physics—competent workman ordinarily employed would produce the effect if directions fairly followed. The specification should enable without requiring invention or addition by the workman. (Text: 'the law means to adopt ... the ability of skilful practical workmen ... to practise the invention from the directions given.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher scientific witnesses may also be competent
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be another class of witnesses—persons with thorough scientific or theoretical knowledge—competent to be examined on sufficiency; both practical artisans and theoreticians may fall within 'skilled in the art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While practical workmen are the general standard, higher scientific witnesses of theoretical knowledge may be examined when appropriate. (Text: 'there may be another class of witnesses, of much higher character, competent to be examined on this point.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must teach how the invention is to be carried into effect; cannot set a problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must disclose not only the nature of the invention but how it may be carried into effect; it must not merely suggest a problem that competent workmen must solve by invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If specification leaves workmen to 'set themselves a problem to solve' it is bad; it must enable a competent workman to carry the invention into effect 'without any inventions on his part.' (Text: 'If the invention can only be carried into effect by persons setting themselves a problem to solve... then the specification would be bad.')

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple inventions are claimed, each must be sufficiently specified
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent describes two or more inventions, each invention must be described with sufficient clearness and distinctness to enable a competent workman to carry it into effect; if any one is insufficiently specified, the patent fails as to that invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee who puts multiple inventions in one patent cannot hold unless each can be supported as a separate patent; specification must be fair, open, and sufficient as a quid pro quo for monopoly. (Text: 'He has described two inventions, and if either of those inventions is not sufficiently specified, the patent fails.')

rubrics_metrics.name: If a whole class of substances is claimed, plaintiff must show each will succeed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent claims a whole class of substances as suitable, plaintiff must show that each of them will succeed (i.e., the specification must enable across the claimed class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to show that members of the claimed class work will undermine sufficiency. (Text, footnote: 'And if a whole class of substances be stated as suitable, the plaintiff must show that each of them will succeed.')
